prompt: In a stable M/M/1 queue, mean service time is unchanged as utilisation moves closer to full capacity. What should you expect of mean response time?

options.text: It falls because the server spends less time idle
options.explanation: Less idle capacity means less opportunity to clear bursts; queueing rises.

options.text: It rises only in direct proportion to utilisation
options.explanation: Near saturation, this queue model has a sharply increasing delay curve.

options.text: It rises sharply because much less spare capacity remains to clear queued work
options.explanation: Correct. Mean response time includes waiting; small utilisation increases near saturation can greatly increase it.

options.text: It stays equal to service time until utilisation reaches exactly 100%
options.explanation: Queueing exists below full utilisation; it is not an all-or-nothing threshold.

workedExample: Separate service time from waiting time. The work per request has not changed, but arrivals increasingly find unfinished work ahead. In this model shrinking idle capacity increases mean waiting sharply. Its arrival/service and single-server assumptions do not predict every production system.

link.title: Using load shedding to avoid overload (AWS Builders' Library)

prompt: A service’s mean response time meets its target, but a small group of users still waits much longer. An M/M/1 model illustrates a long response-time tail. What is the right conclusion?

options.text: A mean target guarantees the p99 target too
options.explanation: The mean does not bound the slowest users.

options.text: Every production service has exactly the M/M/1 tail multiplier
options.explanation: Different service distributions, parallelism and scheduling change the tail.

options.text: Measure the latency distribution and reserve headroom for the user-facing tail target
options.explanation: Correct. The model illustrates why a satisfactory mean can coexist with poor tail latency; real measurements decide capacity.

options.text: Ignore queueing and compare only CPU time per request
options.explanation: User latency includes waiting and other delays as well as service work.

workedExample: Mean latency compresses the distribution into one value. In the lesson’s particular model, p99 is much higher than the mean; other systems have different curves. Test the actual percentile or threshold-based SLI under normal load and planned failures.
